title: Crumb: how life builds structure
teaches: How roots, fungi and microbes glue grains into crumbs, why crumbs matter for water and air, and what digging and footsteps do to them

blocks.text: Lift a forkful from an old, well-kept bed and it falls apart into rounded crumbs, from rice-sized to pea-sized, dark and soft, like crumbled chocolate cake. Lift one from a new bed in heavy ground and it comes up as a slab that breaks into sharp-edged clods, or else as loose dust. The grains in all three may be the same. What differs is how they are stuck together: the soil's **structure**.

blocks.caption: Good crumb: dark, rounded and soft, falling apart in the hand

blocks.text: This is where the last four lessons meet. A crumb is [[clay|clay]] and [[silt|silt]] and [[sand|sand]] (lesson 1), held together by [[organic matter|organic]] (lesson 4) and the gums and threads of soil life (lesson 3). Between the crumbs are pores that drain and hold air; inside them are pores that hold water (lesson 2). It is built in layers.[^hierarchy] The smallest crumbs are clay plates and humus bound by electric charges and sticky microbial gums. Fine roots and fungal threads then wrap those into bigger crumbs, like string around a parcel, and coat them with more glue.[^glomalin]

Crumbs do something no texture can. Between them are big pores, even in a clay soil whose grains leave only tiny gaps. So a crumbly clay drains and breathes almost like a loam, while still holding the water and nutrients that clay holds. That is the real reason gardeners can turn a sticky clay into good ground without changing its texture at all.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Structure is how grains are stuck together; crumbs are the good kind.
Crumbs are built by soil life: gums glue the small ones, roots and fungal threads bind the big ones.
The big pores between crumbs let clay soils drain and breathe.

blocks.text: Structure is built by roots, fungi and the microbes that eat organic matter. It lasts only as long as they keep building, because crumbs are always being eaten and broken down too. Here is a loam bed. Give it roots, organic matter and peace, or take them away.

blocks.caption: The same loam, magnified, under different care
blocks.task: Build strong crumb, and keep it

blocks.text: Digging is the surprise for most people. A freshly dug bed *looks* loose and airy, and for a few weeks it is. But digging slices fungal threads and breaks crumbs. It lets in a rush of air, so microbes burn through the organic matter that holds the crumbs together. After a few rains, a dug bed slumps tighter than before, and digging it again is the only way to loosen it: a habit that feeds itself.

Footsteps are worse, especially on wet soil, where water lets the grains slide past each other and pack.[^wet-soil] One footprint on a wet clay bed can press a hard layer that lasts all summer. Before you work a bed, squeeze a handful: if it smears or stays in a sticky lump, it is too wet, and a few dry days will save you a summer. The cheapest improvement in most gardens is a path: beds narrow enough to reach the middle from the side, and nobody walking on them, ever.

If a bed is already packed hard, loosen it once and then protect it. Push a garden fork in to its full depth and rock it back to crack the soil, without turning it over, every 15 cm or so across the bed. Then keep off it and mulch it, and let roots and worms hold the cracks open. Deep-rooted cover crops such as radishes (lesson 7) carry on the work.

There is a simple way to see how strong your crumbs are. Drop a dry one into water. Water rushes into its pores, squeezing the air inside, and pushes on the crumb from within. A crumb held only by its own stickiness bursts apart into mud. One held by roots, threads and gums survives, sometimes for hours.

blocks.caption: Two dry clods of the same loam from two beds, dropped into water and five minutes later: same grains, different glue

blocks.title: Try it in the garden
points: **The slake test.** Let a few walnut-sized lumps from the top 5 cm of each bed dry on a windowsill for a day. Set each on a square of wire mesh or a kitchen sieve resting just under the water in a clear glass, and watch for five minutes. See whether it holds, crumbles at the edges, or melts.
**The screwdriver test.** When the soil is moist, push a long screwdriver or a stiff wire straight down. Where it suddenly stops being easy, you have hit a compacted layer. Note how deep.
**The spade test.** Lift a spadeful and look at its side. Rounded crumbs with roots running through them are good. Flat plates or big sharp-edged blocks, and roots bending sideways, mean compaction.

blocks.caption: Eight questions on crumb and structure

items.question: What holds the grains of a good crumb together?
options: Microbial gums, humus, fine roots and fungal threads
Only the weight of the soil above
Sand grains locking together
items.why: Small crumbs are glued by gums and humus bound to clay; roots and fungal threads bind them into bigger ones.

items.question: How can a clay soil drain well without changing its texture?
options: Strong crumbs leave big pores between them
Clay always drains well
By digging in a little sand
items.why: Clay grains alone leave only tiny pores, but crumbs of clay have big pores between them that drain and hold air.

items.question: A bed is dug every spring and looks wonderfully loose. Why does it slump tight after a few rains?
options: Digging broke crumbs and sped up the loss of the organic matter holding them
The rain added clay
It was not dug deeply enough
items.why: Digging slices fungal threads and lets air in, and microbes burn the organic matter that glues crumbs. The fluffiness doesn't last.

items.question: When does a footstep do most damage to a bed?
options: When the soil is wet
When it is dry
When it is frozen
items.why: Water lets the grains slide past each other, so wet soil packs much more under the same weight.

items.question: In a slake test, a dry clod melts into mud within seconds. What does that say?
options: Its crumbs are weak: little life and organic matter holding them
It is a very healthy soil
It is pure sand
items.why: Strong crumbs, glued by roots, fungi and gums, hold together in water. Weak ones burst as water pushes in.

items.question: A screwdriver slides in easily and then stops dead 15 cm down. What is there?
options: A compacted layer
The water table
Good crumbly soil
items.why: A sudden stop means a dense layer, often pressed by footsteps, machines or digging to the same depth every year.

items.question: A screwdriver test finds a hard layer 15 cm down. What is a good first fix?
options: Rock a fork through it once without turning the soil, then keep off and mulch
Dig the bed over every spring from now on
Roll the bed flat
items.why: One gentle loosening cracks the layer without burying the topsoil or tearing up all its crumbs. Mulch, roots and worms then keep it open, as long as nobody treads on it.

items.question: What is the cheapest way to protect the structure of a bed?
options: Never walk on it: use paths
Dig it twice a year
Leave it bare so it dries
items.why: Keeping feet off the beds stops compaction at its source. Beds narrow enough to reach the middle make it easy.

learned: Structure is how grains are stuck into crumbs; crumbs leave big pores that drain and breathe.
Roots, fungal threads, microbial gums and humus build crumbs, in layers from small to large.
Digging breaks crumbs and burns the organic matter that glues them; footsteps on wet soil pack it hard. Loosen a packed bed once with a fork, then keep off it.
The slake, screwdriver and spade tests show how strong a soil's crumbs are and where it is compacted.

hierarchy.title: Aggregate hierarchy
hierarchy.text: Crumbs are **aggregates**. Judith Tisdall and Malcolm Oades described the layers in 1982: **microaggregates**, under a quarter of a millimetre, held by clay, humus and charged metals, and **macroaggregates**, bigger ones, held by roots and fungal threads. The big ones are the first to break and the first to rebuild.

glomalin.title: Glomalin
glomalin.text: In 1996 Sara Wright, at the US Department of Agriculture, found a sticky protein on mycorrhizal fungal threads, which she named **glomalin**, and it was hailed as the soil's superglue. Later work found that what the test measures is a mixture, not one protein. The broad point stands: fungi help hold crumbs together, with their threads and with what they leave behind.

wet-soil.title: Why wet soil packs
wet-soil.text: A soil packs most easily at a moisture a little drier than field capacity: wet enough that water films let grains slide past each other, not so wet that water fills the pores and pushes back. In practice: if a ball of soil squeezed in the hand smears or stays in a sticky lump, keep off it.
